claims.text: A conventional low-alloy steel susceptible to temper embrittlement can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition after treatment within a narrow temperature window.
The transition is induced by temperature-dependent segregation of embrittling impurities such as phosphorus to grain boundaries.
Mo- or Cr-containing conventional low-alloy steel with trace impurities is an appropriate initial material for the proposed transition.
Homogenization can provide an initial state in which the trace impurities have not yet segregated significantly.
A controlled thermal treatment can activate impurity segregation within an intermediate temperature window and deactivate or reverse its effect outside that window.
Intermediate temperatures favor significant grain-boundary impurity segregation, whereas lower and higher temperatures do not.
Impurity atoms such as phosphorus segregate to grain boundaries in the intermediate-temperature regime.
At intermediate temperatures, impurity mobility is sufficient to cause impurity accumulation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary impurity accumulation lowers intergranular cohesion.
Reduced intergranular cohesion causes brittle behavior.
At lower or higher temperatures, suppressed segregation or changes in solubility minimize grain-boundary embrittlement.
The proposed steel will have relatively high ductility at low and high temperatures but markedly lower ductility and toughness in the intermediate temper-embrittlement range.
Avoiding impurity segregation in the same alloy provides a non-embrittled baseline.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys do not display the proposed temper-embrittlement-associated ductile–brittle–ductile behavior.
The phenomenon requires sufficient impurity content and appropriate segregation kinetics in a conventional alloy.
The temperature range and magnitude of embrittlement depend on alloy composition, impurity content, and segregation kinetics.
